steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on source-free graph domain adaptation, where a GNN trained on a labelled source graph has to be adapted to an unlabelled target graph without access to the source data. Motivate the problem, review existing graph domain adaptation methods and their limits, sketch our GraphCTA framework, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Graphs on the Web, GNNs, cost of labels, domain adaptation
- Existing unsupervised graph domain adaptation: discrepancy minimization vs adversarial
- Privacy problem: motivating example (financial institution)
- Challenges of source-free adaptation on graphs; SOGA's limits
- GraphCTA: model-view and graph-view adaptation in a loop
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Web as network of entities -> graphs
  - graph techniques in web apps: online article classification (cite), web-scale recommendation (cite), anomaly detection (cite)
  - GNNs effective for graph-structured data (cite)
  - needs sufficient high-quality labels; labelling graphs laborious, time-consuming
  - e.g. molecular graph properties need chemical expertise, lab analysis (cite)
  - domain adaptation: transfer knowledge from labelled source to unlabelled target
  - but source-trained GNNs degrade on target due to domain discrepancies (cite)
  - lots of work on domain invariant representations
- Two mainstream strategies for unsupervised graph DA
  - explicitly minimize distribution discrepancy (cite); choice of metric matters
  - common metrics: maximum mean discrepancy (cite), central moment discrepancy (cite)
  - adversarial training with domain discriminator (cite); implicit alignment, no predefined metric -> popular
  - both need source data access -> privacy, intellectual concerns
  - practice: only unlabelled target data + source-pretrained model = source-free unsupervised DA
- Example: global financial institution
  - many domestic and overseas transactions; sensitive customer info
  - privacy regulations restrict access across countries: EU GDPR, Singapore PDPA
  - source-free: adapt fraud detection model from domestic graph to overseas graphs
  - joint methods not applicable here
- Challenges
  - source-free DA studied for image and text (cite); little for non-iid graphs
  - (1) adapt without labelled source graph? (2) shifts from node features and graph structure?
  - citation network example: AI and LLMs popular -> features (paper contents) and structure (citations) change over time; earlier version (before 2010) vs recent (after 2010)
  - no labels -> source hypothesis bias, false predictions on target
  - SOGA (cite): only local neighbor similarity in target, ignores global info and inherent graph discrepancy
  - need graph-specific source-free techniques
- GraphCTA (Collaborate To Adapt)
  - bi-directional adaptation: GNN model view + graph data view
  - node representations from selected neighborhoods and complemented features
  - model-view adaptation: local neighborhood predictions + global class prototypes
  - memory banks (cite) store target representations and predictions, momentum updating -> robust prototypes, consistent predictions
  - graph-view adaptation: filter noisy neighbors, complement features using predictions + memory banks
  - pseudo labels from high-confidence targets; neighborhood contrastive learning
  - updated graph feeds next round of model adaptation -> collaborative loop
  - evaluated on multiple benchmarks; can beat source-needed baselines
- Contributions
  - investigate source-free unsupervised graph DA; practical, less explored
  - first to do model and graph adaptation collaboratively; architecture-agnostic
  - beats SOTA baselines by 2.14% on average

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Web is a complicated network of entities that are connected to each other, and it can be represented well with graph structures. Graph techniques have shown impressive performance in many web applications, like online article classification, web-scale recommendation systems, and anomaly detection, etc. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have clearly become an effective tool for graph-structured data in many applications. But this success usually depends on having enough high-quality labels. Getting enough labels for graph-structured data can be laborious and take a lot of time. For example, to annotate the properties of molecular graphs you need expertise in chemistry and rigorous laboratory analysis. Domain adaptation is an appealing way to reduce this annotation burden, because it transfers the key knowledge from a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain. However, GNN models trained on source domains usually lose a lot of performance when they are deployed directly on target domains, because of domain discrepancies. A lot of effort has gone into learning domain invariant representations, so that the model can generalize better to different domains.

Recently two main strategies have been explored for unsupervised graph domain adaptation. The first one explicitly minimizes the distribution discrepancies between the source and target representations. For these methods, how to define a good discrepancy metric is important. Two measures that are commonly used to match representations across domains are the maximum mean discrepancy and the central moment discrepancy. The second direction uses adversarial training to get domain invariant representations, and it aligns the representations implicitly through a domain discriminator. It has become more popular because it is flexible and does not need a predefined metric. But these joint learning approaches all need permission to access the source data, which is a big challenge for data privacy and intellectual concerns. In most practical scenarios, the only resources available for domain adaptation are unlabelled target data and a model pretrained on the source, and this is called source-free unsupervised domain adaptation.

For example, imagine a financial institution that operates globally and processes many transactions from domestic and overseas sources. Because these transactions involve sensitive customer information, privacy regulations such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR) and Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), etc. restrict the institution's access to transaction data across countries. With source-free graph adaptation, the institution can adapt fraud detection models trained on the domestic transaction graph so they work on overseas graphs, while still respecting the privacy regulations that limit sharing transaction data between countries. The domain adaptation models mentioned before cannot be used here, because accessing and using the labelled source data raises big privacy concerns.

- Challenges
  - source-free DA well studied for image/text, little for non-iid graphs
  - (1) adapt without labelled source graph? (2) shifts from node features and structure?
  - citation network example: AI/LLMs; paper contents and citations change; before 2010 vs after 2010
  - no labels -> source hypothesis bias, false predictions
  - SOGA: only local neighbor similarity, ignores global info and graph discrepancy
- GraphCTA (Collaborate To Adapt)
  - bi-directional: model view + graph view
  - selected neighborhoods, complemented features
  - model-view: local neighborhood predictions + global class prototypes; memory banks with momentum updating
  - graph-view: filter noisy neighbors, complement features; pseudo labels, neighborhood contrastive learning
  - updated graph -> next model round, collaborative loop
  - multiple benchmarks, beats even source-needed baselines
- Contributions: new practical problem; first collaborative model+graph adaptation, architecture-agnostic; +2.14% avg over SOTA

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The Web is a complicated network of entities that are connected to each other, and it can be represented well with graph structures. Graph techniques have shown impressive performance in many web applications, like online article classification, web-scale recommendation systems, and anomaly detection, etc. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have clearly become an effective tool for graph-structured data in many applications. But this success usually depends on having enough high-quality labels. Getting enough labels for graph-structured data can be laborious and take a lot of time. For example, to annotate the properties of molecular graphs you need expertise in chemistry and rigorous laboratory analysis. Domain adaptation is an appealing way to reduce this annotation burden, because it transfers the key knowledge from a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain. However, GNN models trained on source domains usually lose a lot of performance when they are deployed directly on target domains, because of domain discrepancies. A lot of effort has gone into learning domain invariant representations, so that the model can generalize better to different domains.

Recently two main strategies have been explored for unsupervised graph domain adaptation. The first one explicitly minimizes the distribution discrepancies between the source and target representations. For these methods, how to define a good discrepancy metric is important. Two measures that are commonly used to match representations across domains are the maximum mean discrepancy and the central moment discrepancy. The second direction uses adversarial training to get domain invariant representations, and it aligns the representations implicitly through a domain discriminator. It has become more popular because it is flexible and does not need a predefined metric. But these joint learning approaches all need permission to access the source data, which is a big challenge for data privacy and intellectual concerns. In most practical scenarios, the only resources available for domain adaptation are unlabelled target data and a model pretrained on the source, and this is called source-free unsupervised domain adaptation.

For example, imagine a financial institution that operates globally and processes many transactions from domestic and overseas sources. Because these transactions involve sensitive customer information, privacy regulations such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR) and Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), etc. restrict the institution's access to transaction data across countries. With source-free graph adaptation, the institution can adapt fraud detection models trained on the domestic transaction graph so they work on overseas graphs, while still respecting the privacy regulations that limit sharing transaction data between countries. The domain adaptation models mentioned before cannot be used here, because accessing and using the labelled source data raises big privacy concerns.

Source-free unsupervised domain adaptation has been studied a lot for image and text data, but there has not been much work on source-free adaptation for non-iid graph-structured data. There are two main challenges in this setting: (1) How can we adapt without access to the labelled source graph? (2) How can we deal with distribution shifts caused by node features and also by graph structures? For example, in citation networks, when a research field becomes more popular, like the rise of artificial intelligence and large language models, the node features (the contents of the papers) and the graph structures (the citation relationships between papers) can change a lot over time. Because of the complex interactions between nodes, it is hard to adapt a GNN model trained on an earlier version of the citation network (e.g., before 2010) to a more recent version (e.g., after 2010). Also, without graph labels for supervision, the semantic patterns learned from the source graph may not fit the target graph, so there is source hypothesis bias and the model makes false predictions on the target graph. One recent work, SOGA, does source-free domain adaptation on graphs, but it only looks at local neighbor similarity in the target graph and ignores the global information and the inherent graph discrepancy. So we need source-free graph domain adaptation techniques that deal with the challenges of graph-structured data specifically and overcome the limitations of existing approaches.

To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called GraphCTA (Collaborate To Adapt). It does source-free graph domain adaptation with bi-directional adaptations that collaborate, from the perspective of the GNN model and from the perspective of the graph data. To learn node representations that are invariant to arbitrary unknown distribution shifts, GraphCTA generates node representations with selected node neighborhoods and complemented node features. Then we do model-view adaptation based on the local neighborhood predictions and the global class prototypes. We use memory banks to store all target representations and their predictions with momentum updating, which gives robust class prototypes and keeps predictions consistent during training. We also do graph-view adaptation based on the model's predictions and the information in the memory banks, to filter out noisy neighbors and complement node features. In particular, we get pseudo labels from high-confidence target samples and use neighborhood contrastive learning to guide the graph adaptation. The updated graph is then used as input for the next round of model adaptation, so there is a collaborative loop between model adaptation and graph adaptation. We evaluate GraphCTA on multiple benchmarks and the results show that it is effective, and it can even do better than baselines that need the source data in various scenarios.

Our main contributions are:

- We study source-free unsupervised graph domain adaptation, where labelled source graphs cannot be accessed during target adaptation. This is more practical in real-world scenarios and has not been explored much in the graph neural network literature.

- As far as we know, we are the first to do model adaptation and graph adaptation collaboratively. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and can be used with many GNN architectures.

- Extensive experiments show our model is effective, and GraphCTA beats the SOTA baselines by 2.14% on average across multiple settings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The Web is a complicated network of interconnected entities, which can be effectively represented using graph structures. Graph techniques have shown impressive performance in various web applications such as online article classification [1,2], web-scale recommendation systems [3,4], and anomaly detection [5,6], etc. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have undoubtedly become an effective tool for handling graph-structured data across various applications [7,8]. Despite this success, the performance improvement often comes at the cost of requiring sufficient high-quality labels. Unfortunately, obtaining enough labels for graph-structured data can be a laborious and time-consuming task. For instance, annotating the properties of molecular graphs requires expertise in chemical domains and rigorous laboratory analysis [9]. To alleviate the burden of data annotation, domain adaptation offers an appealing way to transfer the key knowledge obtained from a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain. However, GNN models trained on source domains typically suffer significant performance degradation when directly deployed to target domains, due to domain discrepancies [10,11,12]. Considerable effort has been devoted to learning domain invariant representations, thereby improving the model's ability to generalize to different domains.

Recently, two mainstream strategies have been explored for unsupervised graph domain adaptation. One line of research explicitly minimizes the distribution discrepancies between source and target representations [13,14,15]. Defining an appropriate discrepancy metric plays an important role in this kind of method. Two commonly adopted measures for matching cross-domain representations are the maximum mean discrepancy [16] and the central moment discrepancy [17]. Another direction uses adversarial training to obtain domain invariant representations [18,19,20], achieving implicit representation alignment through a domain discriminator. Its flexibility in not requiring a predefined metric has made it increasingly popular. Nonetheless, these joint learning approaches require authorization to access the source data, which poses great challenges regarding data privacy and intellectual concerns. In most practical scenarios, the only resources accessible for domain adaptation are unlabelled target data and a source-pretrained model, a setting known as source-free unsupervised domain adaptation.

Imagine a financial institution that operates globally, processing a large number of transactions from domestic and overseas sources. Given the sensitivity of the customer information involved, privacy regulations such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR) and Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), etc., restrict the institution's access to transaction data across countries. With source-free graph adaptation, the institution can adapt fraud detection models trained on the domestic transaction graph to overseas graphs, while respecting the privacy regulations that limit sharing transaction data across countries. The domain adaptation models mentioned above, by contrast, are not applicable here due to the significant privacy concerns of accessing and using the labelled source data.

While source-free unsupervised domain adaptation has been extensively studied for image and text data [21,22,23,24,25], source-free adaptation techniques for non-iid graph-structured data have received limited investigation. Two primary challenges arise in this scenario: (1) How can adaptation be achieved without access to the labelled source graph? (2) How can distribution shifts induced by both node features and graph structures be mitigated? For instance, in citation networks, when a research field gains popularity, such as with the rise of artificial intelligence and large language models, the node features (i.e., the contents of the papers) and graph structures (i.e., the citation relationships between the papers) may change significantly over time. The complex interactions among nodes make it very challenging to adapt a GNN model trained on an earlier version of the citation network (e.g., before 2010) to a more recent version (e.g., after 2010). Meanwhile, without graph labels for supervision, the semantic patterns learned from the source graph may not suit the target graph, which suffers from source hypothesis bias and leads to false predictions on the target graph. One recent work, SOGA [26], performs source-free domain adaptation on graphs, but it focuses only on local neighbor similarity within the target graph, overlooking global information and the inherent graph discrepancy. Hence, source-free graph domain adaptation techniques are needed that specifically tackle the challenges posed by graph-structured data while overcoming the limitations of existing approaches.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework, GraphCTA (Collaborate To Adapt), which achieves source-free graph domain adaptation through collaborative bi-directional adaptations from the perspectives of the GNN model and the graph data. Specifically, to learn node representations invariant to arbitrary unknown distribution shifts, GraphCTA generates node representations with selected node neighborhoods and complemented node features. We then perform model-view adaptation based on local neighborhood predictions and global class prototypes. Memory banks [27] store all target representations and their corresponding predictions through momentum updating, producing robust class prototypes and ensuring consistent predictions during training. To filter out noisy neighbors and complement node features, we further conduct graph-view adaptation based on the model's predictions and the information stored in the memory banks. In particular, we derive pseudo labels from high-confidence target samples and use neighborhood contrastive learning to guide graph adaptation. Using the updated graph as input enables the next round of model adaptation, establishing a collaborative loop between model and graph adaptation. We evaluate GraphCTA comprehensively on multiple benchmarks, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness; it can even outperform source-needed baselines in various scenarios.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

- • We investigate source-free unsupervised graph domain adaptation without access to labelled source graphs during target adaptation, a problem that is more practical in real-world scenarios and less explored in the graph neural network literature.

- • To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to perform model adaptation and graph adaptation collaboratively; our approach is architecture-agnostic and applicable to numerous GNN architectures.

- • Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our model, with GraphCTA outperforming the SOTA baselines by an average of 2.14% across multiple settings.
